            Rebecca Lawn
          
        
        Research Associate
        
        
          
            
              Read Bio
              
                Dr. Lawn is a Research Associate in the School of Population and Public Health. Previously, she was a Research Associate in the Department of Epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Dr. Lawn gained a first-class BSc (Hons) in Psychology from Newcastle University and received her Ph.D. from the University of Bristol, where she worked between the School of Psychological Science and the MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit. Dr. Lawn’s Ph.D. research applied genetic methods such as Mendelian randomization to investigate the causes and consequences of reproductive traits. Her current research focuses on women’s health over the life course and diseases of aging, with a particular interest in the link between experiences of gender-based violence and later life cardiovascular disease.

              
            
          
        
      
    
  
    
      
        
      
      
        
          
            Amanda Kurowski
          
        
        PhD Student
        
        
          
            
              Read Bio
              
                I am a graduate student in the Genome Science and Technology (GSAT) program at UBC, co-supervised by Dr. Silvia Stringhini and Dr. Michael Kobor. I hold a Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BScN) from the University of Alberta and a Master of Public Health (MPH) from Simon Fraser University. I also work as a nurse at the BC Drug and Poison Information Centre.

My current research explores how socioeconomic factors, such as income, and environmental exposures, such as pollution, contribute to biological aging as captured by epigenetic markers.

Outside the lab, I enjoy exploring the great outdoors of BC, spending time with my family, and traveling.

            Kalia Bennett
          
        
        PhD Student
        
        
          
            
              Read Bio
              
                Kalia is a current PhD student in Population and Public Health at SPPH supervised by Dr. Silvia Stringhini. She holds a Bachelor of Medical Science (BMSc) specializing in Epidemiology and Biostatistics from Western University. Her past research helped to identify factors that affect the efficiency and equity of healthcare quality across different populations. Her doctoral thesis focuses on understanding pathways for how social and environmental conditions impact health and aging outcomes in early-life. She aims to analyze how both individual and neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage becomes biologically embedded through biomarker and omics measures, including estimates of biological age.

              Read Bio
              
                Keenan is a Research Scientist working with the Stringhini Laboratory at UBC’s School of Population and Public Health. Before joining UBC, he completed his BSc in Molecular Biology and MSc in Parasitology at Simon Fraser University. His work with the Stringhini lab examines the biological and health implications of different exposures across the lifespan to better understand which environments, systems, and behaviours support healthier ageing trajectories.

title: Research
text:
Our research centres on social inequalities in ageing across the life course, and on the biological, environmental, and structural mechanisms that produce them. Current directions include:
Unequal ageing trajectories — how socioeconomic circumstances across the life course shape the rate and timing of decline in physical function, cognition, and multisystem health, and which exposures explain the divergence between social groups. This work uses harmonised cross-national cohort data to compare how ageing gradients differ across welfare and policy contexts, and is supported by a CIHR program on environmental pathways, protective factors, and actionable levers in unequal ageing.
Biological embedding of social disadvantage — epigenetic clocks, allostatic load, inflammation, telomere length, and multi-omic markers of accelerated ageing, examined from birth through later life to identify when and how social adversity registers biologically.
Environmental pathways to health inequalities — the contribution of environmental exposures (air pollution, heavy metals, wildfire smoke) to social gradients in biological ageing and child health.
Parental leave policy and health inequalities — Canada’s successive parental leave reforms (1990, 2000, and the 2017 extended-benefit option) offer a natural experiment for evaluating whether a major public investment in the early-life window narrows or widens health gaps. Because uptake of extended leave is strongly patterned by income, employment security, and employer top-ups, its benefits may concentrate among more advantaged families. This work uses the Canadian Community Health Survey, the Discharge Abstract Database, the BC Early Development Instrument, and the Parental Experiences Survey to estimate short- and long-term effects on maternal and child health across the socioeconomic gradient.
Intersectionality and cumulative disadvantage — quantitative approaches (e.g., MAIHDA) to how socioeconomic status, migration, and racialization jointly shape health across the life course.

title: Research Opportunities
text:
The Stringhini Lab is accepting MSc and PhD enquiries

We are looking for students with a solid background in epidemiology and quantitative methods, and welcome enquiries in the following areas:

social and environmental determinants of ageing trajectories, using longitudinal cohort data
environmental and social pathways to biological ageing, using epigenetic and multi-omic data
early-life environmental exposures (wildfire smoke, air pollution, heavy metals) and their social patterning
quasi-experimental evaluation of policy changes on inequalities in health.

Applicants should have formal training in epidemiology, biostatistics, or a related quantitative discipline, and be comfortable working with large longitudinal datasets. Familiarity with causal inference, mediation, or quasi-experimental methods, and proficiency in R or Python, are strong assets. Interest in life-course and biological-embedding frameworks is important. Enquiries should include a CV, a brief statement of research interests, and an indication of which project area is the best fit.


Please see our Research page for current projects in our research group and our Selected Publications page for research examples.

The Health Impact of Parental Leave: Assessing the Effect of Policy Changes and Leave Uptake on Short- and Long-Term Maternal and Child Health Outcomes in Canada


Stringhini, Silvia; Guhn, Martin; Mah, Sarah M; McDade, Thomas


Canadian Institutes of Health Research


Parental leave policies provide time off work after childbirth and play an important role in supporting families and health. Research shows that paid leave improves short-term outcomes, such as reducing postpartum depression, lowering maternal hospital readmissions, and supporting early child development. However, we know much less about the long-term health effects of parental leave and whether it helps reduce health inequalities. This study will examine how the 2000 policy reform in Canada affected mothers’ physical and mental health in both the short and long term, including depression, hospital stays, and overall health years after childbirth. It will also assess how the 2000 and 2017 reforms influenced children’s early development and their health through adolescence and early adulthood.

Unequal Ageing Trajectories Across the Life Course: Environmental Pathways, Protective Factors, and Actionable Levers


Stringhini, Silvia; Kobor, Michael S; McLeod, Christopher B


Canadian Institutes of Health Research


This project aims to provide crucial insights into how socioeconomic conditions throughout life influence the aging process and contribute to health disparities in later years. Aging outcomes-such as functional decline, disease onset, and biological aging-vary significantly across individuals, with those exposed to adverse socioeconomic conditions, such as poverty or low education, facing a greater risk of poor health as they age.

Socio-economic conditions and functional health trajectories in middle to old age: exploring the role of behavioural and environmental factors


Stringhini, Silvia; Kobor, Michael S


Catalyst Grant - Canadian Institutes of Health Research


Ageing trajectories vary between individuals, with some people ageing faster than others. This project will assess the role of socio-economic conditions in shaping trajectories of physical functioning using data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Ageing. It will examine the extent to which favorable lifestyle and environmental exposures buffer the effect of poor socio-economic circumstances on physical functioning.

title: The Stringhini Laboratory
text:
Welcome to the Stringhini Laboratory

We are a epidemiological research group out of the School of Population and Public Health at UBC and the Edwin S.H. Leong Centre for Healthy Aging. Our research focuses on the social, environmental, and economic factors driving chronic diseases and aging, using a life-course epidemiological approach.
